title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
directAnswer: Use two pointers separated by a gap of n nodes, both starting from a dummy node placed before the head. Advance fast by n steps first, then move fast and slow together until fast hits the end. Slow now sits exactly one node before the target, so slow.next = slow.next.next splices it out. The dummy node makes removing the head itself a non-special case. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Two pointers with a fixed gap of n + a dummy node
remember.formula:
dummy = ListNode(0, head)
slow = fast = dummy
for _ in range(n): fast = fast.next   # open the gap
while fast.next: slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next
slow.next = slow.next.next            # unlink target
return dummy.next
rules: Anchor both pointers at a **dummy** before head so deleting the first node uses the same code path.
Advance `fast` exactly **n** steps to open the gap, then move both until `fast.next` is null — `slow` lands just before the target.
Return `dummy.next`, not `head` — the head may have been the node you removed.
Loop condition is `fast.next != null` (not `fast != null`) so `slow` stops one node *before* the target, not on it.
The gap of n between slow and fast is the whole trick: it converts 'nth from the end' into 'nth ahead of slow'.
whenToUse: Delete or locate a node a fixed distance from the end in a single pass
Any 'nth from the end' query on a singly linked list without precomputing the length
Sliding a fixed-width window of pointers along a list
Problems where a dummy node removes head-deletion edge cases
antiSignals: You already know the length cheaply → a single index from the front is simpler
It's a doubly linked list with a tail pointer → walk back n from the tail directly
You need every node's distance-from-end, not just one → a length pass may be clearer
remember.takeaway: Opening a fixed gap between two pointers turns a two-pass length-then-delete into one clean pass. The dummy-node trick that neutralises head deletion shows up across linked-list editing problems.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can do it in one pass with the gap-of-n two-pointer trick, and whether you use a dummy node to handle removing the head without a special branch.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Stopping slow on the target instead of one before it, or not using a dummy node and crashing/returning wrong when the head is removed.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Do it in a single pass, justify the dummy node by walking through the 'remove the head' case, and confirm the loop condition leaves slow exactly one node before the target.

problemStatement:
Given the `head` of a linked list, remove the `n`-th node from the end of the list and return its head.

Follow up: Could you do this in one pass?
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is sz
understanding: Count n from the tail (n = 1 is the last node) and unlink that node. The constraint guarantees n is valid, so the node always exists. The head itself can be the node to remove — that's the case a dummy node makes painless.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is n guaranteed to be within bounds?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the constraints say 1 ≤ n ≤ sz, so I don't need to validate n against the list length.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can n point at the head (n equals the list length)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, and that's exactly why I use a dummy node before the head — removing the first node then needs no special case.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I do it in one pass or is two passes acceptable?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The follow-up asks for one pass; the two-pointer gap method achieves it. I can mention the simpler two-pass length-then-delete as the baseline.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is n counted 1-based from the end?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — n = 1 means the last node, n = 2 the second-to-last, and so on.

approaches.name: Two Passes — Compute Length, Then Delete
approaches.whenToMention: State it first as the obvious baseline, then offer the one-pass two-pointer version the follow-up asks for.
hints: If you knew the list's length L, which position from the front is the nth node from the end?
The nth-from-end node is at index L - n from the front (0-based). To delete it you need the node just before it, at index L - n - 1.
Pass 1: walk the whole list to get L. Pass 2: from a dummy, step L - n times to reach the predecessor, then splice.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two linear scans (length, then predecessor) → O(2n) = O(n) time. Only a counter and a couple of pointers → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
We turn 'nth from the end' into 'a known index from the front' by first measuring the list.

**Pass 1 — measure.** Walk from head to null counting nodes; call the total `L`. Now the node to remove is the `(L − n)`-th from the front (0-based), and its predecessor is at index `L − n − 1`.

**Pass 2 — delete.** Start at a dummy node placed before the head and step forward `L − n` times. That lands us on the predecessor of the target (the dummy contributes the `−1` so the arithmetic is clean even when the head is removed). A single `prev.next = prev.next.next` unlinks the target.

**Why the dummy still matters here.** If the head is the node to remove (`n == L`), then `L − n = 0` and we step zero times, leaving us on the dummy whose `next` is the head — exactly the predecessor we need. Without the dummy we'd special-case `head = head.next`.

**Why we still prefer one pass.** This is perfectly correct and easy to reason about, but it touches the list twice. The follow-up explicitly asks for a single pass, which the gap-based two-pointer method delivers — same complexity class, one traversal.
approaches.insight: Converting an end-relative index into a front-relative one via the length is the most direct reading of the problem. It's the baseline that motivates the slicker single-pass trick, and the dummy node already earns its keep on the head-removal case.

code.python:
def removeNthFromEnd(self, head: ListNode, n: int) -> ListNode:
    length = 0
    cur = head
    while cur:
        length += 1
        cur = cur.next
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev = dummy
    for _ in range(length - n):
        prev = prev.next
    prev.next = prev.next.next
    return dummy.next

approaches.name: One Pass — Two Pointers with a Gap of n (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer the follow-up wants. Phrase it as 'keep two pointers n apart so when fast hits the end, slow is right before the target'.
hints: You want the node n from the end, but you only discover the end by walking there. What if a second pointer were already n nodes ahead of the first?
Put both pointers on a dummy node before the head. Advance fast n steps to create a gap of exactly n.
Now move fast and slow together until fast.next is null. The gap is preserved, so slow stops exactly one node before the target — splice with slow.next = slow.next.next.
approaches.complexityReasoning: fast traverses the list once (n steps to open the gap plus the rest), slow trails it — a single combined pass of O(n). Two pointers and a dummy → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
We maintain a constant gap of `n` nodes between two pointers so that the moment `fast` reaches the end, `slow` is automatically parked at the right spot.

**Set up the dummy and the gap.** Both `slow` and `fast` start at a dummy node placed before `head`. We advance `fast` exactly `n` times. Now `fast` is `n` nodes ahead of `slow`.

**March in lockstep.** Move both pointers one step at a time while `fast.next != null`. Because the gap never changes, when `fast` lands on the *last* node, `slow` is sitting exactly `n + 1` nodes from the end counting from the dummy — i.e. on the node *immediately before* the nth-from-end target. That predecessor position is precisely what we need to splice.

**Why `fast.next != null` and not `fast != null`.** We want `slow` to stop on the predecessor, not on the target itself. Stopping `fast` on the last node (rather than walking it to null) leaves `slow` one short of the target — exactly one node before it. Using `fast != null` would overshoot `slow` by one and delete the wrong node.

**Why the dummy is essential.** Consider `n == length` (remove the head). The gap setup puts `fast` on the last node right away while `slow` is still on the dummy; the lockstep loop doesn't run, and `slow.next = slow.next.next` neatly drops the head. Returning `dummy.next` then yields the new head. No special-casing — the dummy absorbs the edge.
approaches.insight: A fixed gap between two pointers is a portable trick: it answers 'nth from the end' without ever computing the length. Pair it with a dummy node and head deletion stops being a special case — the two ideas together make linked-list editing branch-free.

pitfalls: Using while (fast != null) instead of fast.next — slow overshoots and deletes the wrong node.
Omitting the dummy and crashing when the head must be removed.
Advancing fast n+1 or n-1 times, breaking the gap arithmetic.

commonMistakes: Stopping slow on the target node instead of one node before it.
Not using a dummy node, so removing the head needs fragile special handling.
Off-by-one when opening the gap (advancing fast n+1 or n-1 steps).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong loop condition lands slow on the target
commonMistakesDetailed.why: To splice you need the node BEFORE the target. Walking fast all the way to null moves slow one node too far.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: No dummy node breaks head removal
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If the head is the nth-from-end node, there's no predecessor to splice from. A dummy gives the head a predecessor.
